text: Mostly because needs are too easy to argue about. If you start with what a child would need monthly, someone is going to dispute the list, and you are into a fight over clothes, activities, school supplies, and so on. Income-based guidelines cut that out: they take combined income, apply the guidelines percentage table, and you get a number without rebuilding a household budget for every case. That doesn't mean the child's actual expenses are ignored; courts can adjust for things like medical or daycare when they are out of the ordinary. But the standard has to be workable and defensible, and an income ratio is much easier to explain than a speculative needs calculation. So the 'what the child would need' part is usually folded into the formula, not itemized in every case. Which is a bit unfair when a parent feels the child's actual needs are different, but it keeps cases from turning into audits.
